consultation:
Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child’s vision or eyes.
Parent: Actually, our daughter often rubs her eyes when she's trying to focus on something, especially when she's watching TV or playing with her toys. It seems like her eyes get tired easily.

Doctor: Please tell us about problems with your child's hearing or ears.
Parent: We've noticed that sometimes she doesn't respond immediately when we call her name. She appears to be distracted or not paying attention at those moments, which can be a bit concerning.

Doctor: Please tell us about the problems with your child’s teeth.
Parent: Chewing harder foods seems to be challenging for her. She tends to avoid eating meats or crunchy vegetables because they're difficult for her to chew.

Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child’s heart.
Parent: Yes, the pediatrician diagnosed a septal defect in her heart. We're working closely with the cardiologist to monitor and manage this condition effectively.

Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child's hormones.
Parent: N/A.

Doctor: Please tell us about any neurological problem your child has (brain, nerves, muscle tone, fits).
Parent: Our daughter gets exhausted rather quickly when engaging in physical activities. Even simple play can leave her feeling drained after a short while.

Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child's kidneys.
Parent: N/A.

Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child’s immune system (ability to fight infection and vaccination responses).
Parent: N/A.

Doctor: Please tell us about problems with your child’s gastrointestinal system (feeding, stomach, bowel).
Parent: She can be quite picky about food and will often refuse to eat certain things. This has led to some challenges at mealtimes, ensuring she gets a balanced diet.

Doctor: Please use this box to tell us about any other medical problems that you haven’t been able to mention above.
Parent: One notable thing is that she was born with shorter fingers on one hand. We're keeping an eye on how this affects her development and dexterity over time.

## 1) RESPIRATORY

a) How this affects the patient: The patient shows difficulty chewing hard foods, preferring softer options like meats and crunchy vegetables.

b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have seizures, and around 38% have heart conditions, including septal defects.

a) How this affects the patient: The patient rubs her eyes when focusing on something, indicating potential eye strain.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have seizures, and around 38% have heart conditions, including septal defects.

## 7) OPHTHALMOLOGY AND VISION
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has a tendency to rub her eyes when focusing on something, suggesting possible eye strain.

## 8) DERMATOLOGY

b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have seizures, and around 38% have heart conditions, including septal defects.

## 9) DENTAL
a) How this affects the patient: The patient avoids eating meats or crunchy vegetables due to difficulty chewing.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have seizures, and around 38% have heart conditions, including septal defects.

## 10) EDUCATION
a) How this affects the patient: The patient requires extra help in school, though most go to a mainstream primary school.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have seizures, and around 38% have heart conditions, including septal defects.

## 11) BEHAVIOUR AND DEVELOPMENT
a) How this affects the patient: The patient experiences exhaustion quickly when engaging in physical activities, particularly simple play.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have seizures, and around 38% have heart conditions, including septal defects.

a) How this affects the patient: The patient has shorter fingers on one hand, which may affect her development and dexterity over time.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have seizures, and around 38% have heart conditions, including septal defects.

## 13) RECOMMENDATIONS FOR SCREENING AND TREATMENTS
a) Regular dental check-ups: The patient needs regular dental check-ups to ensure proper tooth care and prevent dental issues.
b) Regular hearing reviews to age 5: The patient should undergo regular hearing reviews to detect any hearing problems early.
c) Ophthalmology review: The patient should have regular eye examinations to address any vision issues.
d) Check position of testes in boys: The patient's testes should be monitored for normal descent.
e) Consider a palate review: The patient should be referred for a palate review if there are feeding difficulties or speech concerns.
f) Referral for a cardiac review: The patient should be referred to a cardiologist for ongoing monitoring and management of her septal defect.
g) If nothing is found (or already done) this does not need to be repeated: The patient should not repeat any unnecessary cardiac evaluations.
h) Consider a skeletal review: The patient should have X-rays of the wrist, hips, spine, and skull to assess bone age and identify any abnormalities.
i) Any concerns around asymmetric hip creases in infancy and/or asymmetric or painful gait should prompt medical review: The patient should seek medical evaluation if asymmetry or pain is noted.
j) Consider review and investigation for tethered cord: The patient should undergo MRI scans if clinical concerns arise regarding tethered cord issues.
k) Monitor growth velocity: The patient's height should be monitored to detect any deviations from the expected growth patterns.
l) Consider physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech therapy, and behavioral therapy: The patient may benefit from additional therapies to improve overall functionality and quality of life.

Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child’s vision or eyes.
Parent: Oh, yes... she often squints when trying to focus on things, like when watching TV or playing with toys. It's been worrying me lately, and I'm not sure if it's related to her eyes or something else.

Doctor: Please tell us about problems with your child's hearing or ears.
Parent: She's had otitis media in the past. The doctor said it was an infection and gave her antibiotics. Thankfully, it cleared up quickly.

Doctor: Please tell us about the problems with your child’s teeth.
Parent: Her teeth seem to break or chip very easily. Even when she's eating normal foods like apples or crackers‚ a small piece might chip off. It's making me anxious about her dental health.

Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child’s heart.
Parent: When she plays outside or runs around‚ her breathing gets really fast – faster than I expect for a child her age. Sometimes I worry it might be too much for her‚ but she seems okay otherwise.

Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child's hormones.
Parent: N/A.

Doctor: Please tell us about any neurological problem your child has (brain, nerves, muscle tone, fits).
Parent: There are these... episodes‚ where she just stares off into space. They're really frightening because she doesn't respond for a few seconds. Then‚ she snaps back to normal like nothing happened. It's been happening more often lately‚ and I'm getting really concerned.

Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child's kidneys.
Parent: N/A.

Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child’s immune system (ability to fight infection and vaccination responses).
Parent: N/A.

Doctor: Please tell us about problems with your child’s gastrointestinal system (feeding, stomach, bowel).
Parent: Feeding has become a real challenge. She shows a strong aversion to certain textures or smells‚ which limits what she'll eat. Mealtime can be very stressful because of this.

Doctor: Please use this box to tell us about any other medical problems that you haven’t been able to mention above.
Parent: Yes... she was diagnosed with hip dysplasia. The doctor mentioned something about the socket not forming correctly‚ and we need to keep an eye on it to make sure it doesn't cause long-term issues.

consultation:
Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child’s vision or eyes.
Parent: Oh, yes... our child has hypermetropia, which means his eyes are turned inward slightly. It's been a concern since birth, really. I worry about how it might affect his everyday life, like playing catch or watching TV. We've had multiple appointments with specialists already.

Doctor: Please tell us about problems with your child's hearing or ears.
Parent: There's fluid in his ear, which has caused some discomfort and pain. We've taken him to see an ENT specialist a few times now. They've tried a couple of treatments to clear it out. Poor baby gets so upset when it flares up. 

Doctor: Please tell us about the problems with your child’s teeth.
Parent: His teeth... well, they're very weak, especially the enamel. I make sure he brushes them gently and uses a child-friendly toothpaste. But still, there are cavities. It's hard to see him in pain, even if it's just a small filling. 

Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child’s heart.
Parent: Yes, unfortunately. There's an abnormality with one of the valves. We go back to the cardiologist regularly for check-ups. They monitor it closely to ensure everything stays stable. As a parent, it's terrifying to think about, but we're managing so far. 

Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child's hormones.
Parent: N/A.

Doctor: Please tell us about any neurological problem your child has (brain, nerves, muscle tone, fits).
Parent: He was born with a tethered cord. That's meant lots of monitoring over time to ensure no lasting damage occurred. So far, touch wood, he seems okay, though we do have regular scans to confirm. 

Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child's kidneys.
Parent: N/A.

Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child’s immune system (ability to fight infection and vaccination responses).
Parent: N/A.

Doctor: Please tell us about problems with your child’s gastrointestinal system (feeding, stomach, bowel).
Parent: He experiences bowel problems sometimes. This causes him, and us, a lot of distress. Changing diets and keeping an eye on what he eats helps manage it a bit better. But yes, it's definitely something we need to stay on top of. 

Doctor: Please use this box to tell us about any other medical problems that you haven’t been able to mention above.
Parent: Undescended testes were another thing. Something we discovered after birth and have kept track of ever since. Specialists keep saying it might correct itself over time, but until then, we'll continue these regular hospital visits.
